---
title: Area-Level SAE Modeling (Fay--Herriot)"
subtitle: "A Bayesian spatio-temporal extension"
---

::: {.callout-note title="Theory in brief"}
The Fay--Herriot model treats each direct estimate as a noisy observation of the true area-time quantity:

$$
\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} = \mu_{jt} + e_{jt}, \qquad
e_{jt} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{jt}),
$$

where $\psi_{jt}$ is the sampling variance estimated from the survey design. The latent area-time mean is then modelled using predictors and an area random effect:

$$
\mu_{jt} = \alpha + \mathbf{x}_{jt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j.
$$

Here $u_j$ borrows strength across areas while the target remains the area-time quantity $\mu_{jt}$. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect $v_t$ can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. 
The fitted model gives an area-time estimate by combining the direct estimate with the model prediction:

$$
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{FH}}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu_{jt} \mid \hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt}, x_{jt}).
$$

Here $u_j$ borrows strength across areas while the target remains the area-time quantity $\mu_{jt}$. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect $v_t$ can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup-fh
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
share_label <- label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
pp_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(area_id, "W")) |>
  arrange(area_id)

```

```{r}
#| label: plotting-config
#| echo: false
variance_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.0001)
missing_fill <- "grey85"
diverging_low <- "#2166ac"
diverging_high <- "#b2182b"

map_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  axis.title.y = element_text(
    size = 12,
    face = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    margin = margin(r = 15)
  ),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 9)
)

chart_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
)

map_annotation_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30")
)
```

## Estimation approach {.unnumbered}

{{< include assets/target-estimand.qmd >}}

Area-level SAE starts from the direct estimates created in the previous step. The Fay--Herriot model treats each direct estimate for an area-time cell, an *MSOA-year cell* in this example, as a noisy observation of the underlying frequent-walking rate, using its sampling variance to control how much confidence the model places in that value.

The model then borrows strength across MSOAs and survey years using spatial and temporal random effects, together with scaled MSOA-level predictors from ONS UK Census 2021, including age and sex summaries, population density, car-access household share, working-from-home share, student share, and occupation profile. This stabilises weak or missing direct estimates while retaining survey-design information.

## Prepare modelling data

First we import the complete area-time direct-estimates, then load the area predictors.

```{r}
#| label: load-direct-estimates
direct_walk <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_direct.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    all_of(c(
      "area_id",
      "msoa_name",
      "time_id",
      "direct_estimate",
      "variance",
      "n"
    ))
  )

head(direct_walk)
```
```{r}
#| label: load-area-predictors
area_predictors <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "clean", "areapred_freqwalk.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    all_of(c(
      "area_id",
      "scaled_mean_age_adult",
      "scaled_prob_female",
      "scaled_population_density",
      "scaled_car_access_hhshare",
      "scaled_share_work_from_home",
      "scaled_share_students",
      "scaled_share_routine_semiroutine"
    ))
  )
head(area_predictors)
```

The missing or zero sampling variances of direct estimates need to be handled, because it controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the FH model.

- For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly model predictions.
- Because the outcome is binary (`1` for walking daily, `0` otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of `0` when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-sampling-variance
#| code-fold: false

max_variance <- max(direct_walk$variance[direct_walk$variance > 0], na.rm = TRUE)

direct_walk_model <- direct_walk |>
  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(variance) ~ max_variance,
      variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ variance
    )
  )
```

`INLA` uses numeric indices to encode space and time, so we create `time_inla_id` and `area_inla_id` to index survey years and MSOAs. We also provide an adjacency graph for the structured spatial effect. Here, we use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point.

```{r}
#| label: define-model-index
#| code-fold: false

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels),
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)
```
```{r}
#| label: build-spatial-graph
#| code-fold: false

msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)
```

![](assets/spatial_weights_example.png)

Finally, we assemble the modelling data for `INLA` by comining the direct estimates with the area predictors and the numeric indices for the temporal and spatial effects.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-model-data

model_data <- direct_walk_model |>
  left_join(area_predictors, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  arrange(time_id, area_inla_id)

head(model_data)
```

## Fit and evaluate models

Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct estimation is passed to `INLA` as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight. We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using `INLA`.

| Model | Name | Specifications |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Baseline | Intercept plus independent area effect |
| M1 | +Demographic | M0 plus mean age and proportion female |
| M2 | +Core predictors | M1 plus population density and car-access household share |
| M3 | +All predictors | M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH) |
| M4 | +TempSpatial | M3 plus temporal random walk and BYM2 spatial MSOA effect |

The choice of spatial and temporal models should reflect assumptions about how residual variation is structured across space and time.

| Temporal model | Description |
|---|---|
| `rw1` | First-order random walk: smooths neighbouring time periods. |
| `rw2` | Second-order random walk: smooths changes in the trend over longer time series. |
| `ar1` | Autoregressive effect: assumes correlation decays with time distance, so closer years are more similar than distant years. |

| Spatial model | Description |
|---|---|
| `besag` | Smooths estimates across neighbouring areas, capturing spatially structured residual variation. |
| `bym2` | Updated BYM model with a mixing parameter, `phi`, which indicates how much residual variation is spatially structured. |

With only three survey years, `rw1` is suitable because it smooths neighbouring waves. Spatially, `bym2` is appropriate because it allows the model to borrow strength from neighbouring MSOAs while still capturing unstructured local variability.

```{r}
#| label: fit-fh-models
#| code-fold: false

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare +
  scaled_share_work_from_home +
  scaled_share_students +
  scaled_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare +
  scaled_share_work_from_home +
  scaled_share_students +
  scaled_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Demographic" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +TempSpatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)
```

:::{.callout-note}
When fitting area-level FH models with `INLA`, these arguments are needed:

- `control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)` returns fitted values for every row. In an area-level model, these are the final estimates for each area-time row.
- `scale` passes the inverse sampling variance to `INLA`, so less precise direct estimates get smoothed more.
- `control.family` fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the direct-estimate variances already provide the uncertainty.
- `control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)` requests WAIC for comparing model fit in case of multiple specifications.
:::

To compare the fitted models' overall performance, we use `WAIC` or (Widely Applicable Information Criterion) as a first check. It is a global predictive-fit measure returned by `INLA`; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

```{r}
#| label: compare-fh-waic
model_waic <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
)

model_waic
```

M4 has the lowest WAIC and M0 is clearly the weakest model, suggesting that the full set of demographic, core, and additional area predictors plus spatio-temporal structure gives the best overall fit among the FH specifications.

## Final estimates and uncertainty

To extract the estimates for this model, we take the fitted-value summary from the `INLA` object and bind it back to the area-time rows used in the model fit. For transparency, the output also retains the direct estimates, sample sizes, and direct-estimate variances. The final model estimates are reported with uncertainty, shown here using the width of the posterior 95% credible interval.

```{r}
#| label: extract-fh-final-results
#| code-fold: false

model_output_frame <- model_data |>
  select(area_id, time_id, msoa_name, direct_estimate, variance, n)

fitted_values <- fh_fits[["M4 +TempSpatial"]]$summary.fitted.values |>
  as_tibble()

final_fh_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values) |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    msoa_name,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    n,
    fh_estimate = mean,
    fh_variance = sd^2,
    fh_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
    fh_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
    fh_ci_width = fh_upper - fh_lower
  )

head(final_fh_results)
```
```{r}
#| label: map-fh-final-results
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 16
#| out-width: "100%"

final_fh_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(final_fh_results, by = "area_id")
fh_estimate_limits <- range(final_fh_results$fh_estimate, na.rm = TRUE)
fh_ci_width_limits <- c(0, max(final_fh_results$fh_ci_width, na.rm = TRUE))
fh_wave_years <- sort(unique(final_fh_results$time_id))

plot_fh_estimate <- function(wave) {
  final_fh_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = fh_estimate), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = "magma",
      limits = fh_estimate_limits,
      labels = share_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Share"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_fh_ci_width <- function(wave) {
  final_fh_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = fh_ci_width), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Oranges",
      direction = 1,
      limits = fh_ci_width_limits,
      labels = pp_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "95% CI width"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

fh_estimate_maps <- lapply(fh_wave_years, plot_fh_estimate)
fh_uncertainty_maps <- lapply(fh_wave_years, plot_fh_ci_width)

fh_estimate_maps[[1]] <- fh_estimate_maps[[1]] + ylab("Final estimate")
fh_uncertainty_maps[[1]] <- fh_uncertainty_maps[[1]] + ylab("95% CI width")

for (i in seq_len(length(fh_wave_years) - 1)) {
  fh_estimate_maps[[i]] <- fh_estimate_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  fh_uncertainty_maps[[i]] <- fh_uncertainty_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

wrap_plots(c(fh_estimate_maps, fh_uncertainty_maps), ncol = length(fh_wave_years)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Share of adults who walk for transport daily",
    subtitle = "Spatio-temporal FH model (M4) and 95% CI width",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```

Here we see that the Fay--Herriot estimates produce a more plausible spatial pattern than the direct estimates, with less jagged variation across neighbouring areas and clearer broad regional structure. At the same time, weaker survey coverage can still leave year-specific patterns in the modelled estimates. The generally higher 2023 estimates are consistent with weaker survey coverage in that wave, so the modelled estimates should be read alongside posterior interval widths and original sample sizes.

**Unit-level modelling** seeks to overcome this shortcoming by modelling the individual outcome directly using unit-level predictors present in the survey respondent data.

## Further diagnostics

To better understand how the FH results are produced, we can inspect the contribution of each of the model components. The diagnostics below examine how estimates change as predictors, spatial structure, and temporal structure are added, and then review uncertainty and hyperparameters to understand where the model is borrowing strength most strongly.

```{r}
#| label: collate-fh-model-results

model_output_frame <- model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    msoa_name,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    n
  )

fh_results <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    bind_cols(
      model_output_frame,
      as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)
    ) |>
      transmute(
        model = model_name,
        area_id,
        time_id,
        msoa_name,
        direct_estimate,
        variance,
        n,
        fh_estimate = mean,
        fh_variance = sd^2,
        fh_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
        fh_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
        fh_ci_width = fh_upper - fh_lower
      )
  }
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = names(model_formulas)))
```

### How Fay--Herriot model smoothes direct estimates

We start by comparing the direct estimates with M0, the baseline Fay-Herriot model with no area predictors, spatial structure, or temporal structure to understand how the FH models fundamentally handle noisy direct estimates. 

```{r}
#| label: prepare-fh-baseline-comparison

fh_wide <- fh_results |>
  # One row per area-time cell, with model outputs in separate columns.
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    model,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(fh_estimate, fh_variance),
    names_sep = "__"
  )

direct_to_m0 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    direct_variance = variance,
    variance_change = .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]] - variance
  )

wave_years <- sort(unique(fh_wide$time_id))
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-fh-baseline-comparison
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 12
#| out-width: "100%"

variance_change_limit <- max(abs(direct_to_m0$variance_change), na.rm = TRUE) * .5
direct_variance_limit <- max(direct_to_m0$direct_variance, na.rm = TRUE)

direct_to_m0_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(direct_to_m0, by = "area_id")

plot_m0_variance_change <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m0_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = variance_change), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = diverging_low,
      mid = "white",
      high = diverging_high,
      midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-variance_change_limit, variance_change_limit),
      oob = squish,
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Change"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_direct_variance <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m0_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = direct_variance), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Reds",
      direction = 1,
      limits = c(0, direct_variance_limit),
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Variance"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

variance_change_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_m0_variance_change)
direct_variance_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_direct_variance)

variance_change_maps[[1]] <- variance_change_maps[[1]] +
  ylab("Variance change")
direct_variance_maps[[1]] <- direct_variance_maps[[1]] +
  ylab("Direct variance")

for (i in seq_len(length(wave_years) - 1)) {
  variance_change_maps[[i]] <- variance_change_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  direct_variance_maps[[i]] <- direct_variance_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

direct_to_m0_ranked <- direct_to_m0 |>
  drop_na(variance_change) |>
  group_by(time_id) |>
  arrange(direct_variance, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(variance_rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    time_id,
    variance_rank,
    `Variance change` = variance_change,
    `Variance (direct)` = direct_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(time_id, variance_rank),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  )

direct_to_m0_ranked_plot <- ggplot(
  direct_to_m0_ranked,
  aes(
    x = variance_rank,
    y = value,
    colour = measure
  )
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(time_id), nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = variance_label) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Variance change" = "purple",
    "Variance (direct)" = "red"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "",
    x = "MSOAs sorted by variance",
    y = "Variance",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  chart_text_theme

(wrap_plots(c(variance_change_maps, direct_variance_maps), ncol = 3) /
  direct_to_m0_ranked_plot) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Direct estimates compared with baseline FH model (M0)",
    subtitle = "M0 stabilises noisy direct estimates before adding predictors or spatio-temporal structure",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```
Area-time cells with high sampling variance contain less reliable local information, so M0 pulls them more strongly toward its baseline prediction. The Bayesian FH fit also produces posterior estimates for cells with missing direct estimates or zero/missing variance, allowing sparse or unsampled area-time cells to remain in the output with explicit uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: summarise-fh-missing-direct
fh_wide |>
  filter(is.na(direct_estimate) | is.na(variance)) |>
  transmute(
    `MSOA` = area_id,
    `Wave year` = time_id,
    `Direct estimate` = share_label(direct_estimate),
    `Sampling variance` = round(variance, 6),
    `M0 estimate` = share_label(.data[["fh_estimate__M0 Baseline"]]),
    `M0 posterior variance` = round(
      .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]],
      6
    )
  )
```

### Adding Predictors

After the WAIC comparison, we inspect local estimate changes to see where the model moves the target estimates and whether those movements are substantively plausible. In Fay-Herriot SAE, adding predictors changes the expected value for each area-time cell, and unstable direct estimates are pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions when the predictors are relevant.

For example, moving from M2 to M3 adds the occupation and work-pattern predictors. We map where M3 changes the estimates relative to M2, then summarise the predictor profiles of the areas with the largest upward and downward shifts (top and bottom 10%).

```{r}
#| label: calculate-fh-predictor-change

m2_to_m3 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    estimate_change =
      .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +All predictors"]] -
      .data[["fh_estimate__M2 +Core predictors"]]
  ) |>
  distinct(area_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
```
```{r}
#| label: map-fh-predictor-change
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

m2_to_m3_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(m2_to_m3, by = "area_id")

m2_to_m3_estimate_limit <- quantile(
  abs(m2_to_m3$estimate_change),
  0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

m2_to_m3_map_data |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate_change), colour = "transparent") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = diverging_low,
    mid = "white",
    high = diverging_high,
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-m2_to_m3_estimate_limit, m2_to_m3_estimate_limit),
    oob = squish,
    labels = pp_label,
    na.value = missing_fill,
    name = "Change"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimate change after adding additional predictors",
    subtitle = "M3 minus M2"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme
```
```{r}
#| label: summarise-fh-predictor-change
m2_to_m3_drivers <- model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    work_from_home = scaled_share_work_from_home,
    students = scaled_share_students,
    routine_semiroutine = scaled_share_routine_semiroutine
  ) |>
  distinct(area_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  left_join(m2_to_m3, by = "area_id") |>
  mutate(
    change_group = case_when(
      estimate_change >= quantile(estimate_change, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Raised most with M3",
      estimate_change <= quantile(estimate_change, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Lowered most with M3",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

m2_to_m3_drivers |>
  drop_na(change_group) |>
  group_by(change_group) |>
  summarise(
    `Work from home` = mean(work_from_home, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Students` = mean(students, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Routine or semi-routine` = mean(routine_semiroutine, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
The areas whose estimates are raised most by M3 have higher work-from-home and student shares, and lower routine/semi-routine occupation shares. This pattern is plausible: students and remote workers may have more flexible daily routines, shorter local trips, or lower car dependence, all of which could be associated with more walking for transport.

The coefficient table below reports the fixed-effect terms from the final model M4. Because the predictors are standardised, each coefficient can be read as the expected percentage-point change in daily walking associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in that predictor.

```{r}
#| label: summarise-fh-final-coefficients

fh_fits[["M4 +TempSpatial"]]$summary.fixed |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
  mutate(
    term = recode(
      term,
      `(Intercept)` = "Intercept",
      scaled_mean_age_adult = "Mean age adult",
      scaled_prob_female = "Proportion female",
      scaled_population_density = "Population density",
      scaled_car_access_hhshare = "Car-access household share",
      scaled_share_work_from_home = "Work from home",
      scaled_share_students = "Full-time students",
      scaled_share_routine_semiroutine = "Routine/semi-routine occupations"
    )
  ) |>
  transmute(
    term,
    mean = pp_label(mean),
    lower = pp_label(.data[["0.025quant"]]),
    upper = pp_label(.data[["0.975quant"]])
  )
```

In practice, the decision to pick the right SAE model specification should be assessed holistically using model diagnostics, stepwise changes across models, and domain knowledge regarding the modelled outcome.

### Adding Temporal And Spatial Effects

The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be examined through two diagnostic outputs by `INLA`:

- `tau` is the precision of the random effect, or the inverse of its variance. A higher `tau` means the random effect varies less.
- `phi` is the BYM2 mixing parameter: it indicates how much of the area random effect is assigned to the structured spatial component versus the unstructured component. A value of `0.5` means the structured and unstructured components contribute roughly equally to the area random effect.

```{r}
#| label: diagnose-fh-hyperparameters

fh_fits[["M4 +TempSpatial"]]$summary.hyperpar |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |>
  filter(str_detect(parameter, "time_inla_id|area_inla_id|Phi")) |>
  select(parameter, mean, sd, `0.025quant`, `0.5quant`, `0.975quant`) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

The temporal effect has a higher `tau` than the spatial effect, indicating smaller differences between survey waves than between MSOAs. Meanwhile, the low spatial `phi` (less than `0.5`) indicates that only a small share of the remaining between-area variation follows the spatial weights; most of it remains unstructured.

```{r}
#| label: export-fh-results

write_csv(final_fh_results, file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_fh.csv"))
```
